case.label: A
case.text: A candidate could argue the role lacks S3 read permissions, but the failure is on the AssumeRole call itself, before any S3 permission is evaluated; the caller side already allows sts:AssumeRole, so only the trust policy is missing. Not defensible.

case.label: A
case.text: A candidate who thinks of Organizations as a central grant mechanism might pick the SCP, but an SCP only limits the maximum permissions and never grants access; cross-account access needs both the bucket policy allow and the identity-based allow. Not defensible.

case.label: C
case.text: The sentence about a private certificate authority pulls toward IAM Roles Anywhere, which also avoids long-term credentials, but Roles Anywhere is for workloads outside AWS; on EC2 an instance profile is simpler. The CA sentence is a deliberate distractor (twin of iam-q005), not a second answer. Option A also works but moving to new instances adds overhead that B avoids.

case.label: D
case.text: D gives the same protection, but it needs an attach step for every new monthly account and leaves a gap if the step is missed; attaching at the organization root covers new accounts automatically. A and B fail because account administrators can edit IAM policies and they do not restrict the root user.

case.label: D
case.text: A candidate might think a bucket policy allow can open the prefix, but an explicit Deny in any applicable policy overrides every Allow, so D (and C) cannot work. A works but adds a new role and instances, which is more overhead than removing an obsolete statement.

case.label: B
case.text: IAM users in a hub account with role switching also gives employees one sign-in and central control, so it meets the functional requirements; it loses on overhead because the security team must manage 300 IAM users with long-term passwords and keys plus roles in 40 accounts.

case.label: C
case.text: C meets every functional requirement (identity pool, temporary credentials) and differs from B only in scope; it loses on MOST securely because it allows all S3 actions. D fails because GetFederationToken must be called with long-term IAM user credentials, which the app cannot contain.

case.label: D
case.text: Moving the application to EC2 with an instance profile also removes long-term credentials, but a migration is far more overhead than using the existing private CA with IAM Roles Anywhere. B does not apply because the servers are not EC2 instances.

case.label: D
case.text: A candidate might think the group name instead of the ARN is the fix, but an IAM group cannot be a principal in any form. The most direct fix (naming each analyst's IAM user ARN, or granting through the group's identity-based policy in the same account) is not offered; A is the only option that names a valid principal type, so elimination decides it, which a reviewer may see as a mild cue.

case.label: D
case.text: Moving the administrator role to another account also stops developers from passing it, because PassRole cannot reach a role in another account this way; it meets the security goal but is a large migration compared with narrowing the iam:PassRole resource. B does not stop passing the administrator role at all.

case.label: C
case.text: Listing every member account ID in the bucket policy restricts writes correctly, but it must be updated every week as accounts are created; the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition covers future accounts automatically. B fails because an SCP does not grant access to a resource.

case.label: C
case.text: A new key with the default key policy would let the IAM policy take effect and the reads would succeed, but re-encrypting every object and deleting the old key is far more work than adding one key policy statement. B and D fail because the key policy does not enable IAM policies and a bucket policy cannot grant KMS actions.

case.label: A
case.text: Reading CloudTrail by hand reaches the same least-privilege policy from the same data, so it meets the requirement; it loses only on overhead. B fails because the credential report covers users and credentials, not the actions a role called; D tests permissions, it does not show usage.

case.label: A
case.text: A turns on MFA, which is part of protecting the root user, but it keeps daily root use and the root access key, which best practice says to remove. No other option is defensible; a permissions boundary cannot be set on the root user.

case.label: B
case.text: A candidate might confuse patching the operating system (a customer task on EC2) with the hosts that run S3 and DynamoDB, which are managed services where AWS patches the infrastructure. Not defensible.

case.label: C
case.text: SAML federation from AD FS also uses the existing credentials with no second directory and no password copies, so it meets the functional requirements; it loses on overhead because it needs an AD FS server (not stated to exist) and an identity provider plus roles in each of 40 accounts. D adds a second directory, which the stem rules out.

case.label: C
case.text: B does not say how the boundary is enforced; without a condition on iam:CreateRole that requires the boundary, a developer could create a role without it, so a candidate could argue that only a review (C) actually guarantees the maximum. C is still manual and slow, and the stem asks for least overhead, so B remains the best option; the missing enforcement step is a weakness of the option wording, not a second answer. A also limits other teams in the shared account; D grants nothing because a boundary never grants.

case.label: C
case.text: A role that requires MFA in its trust policy, with s3:DeleteObject removed from the users, also makes deletes depend on MFA, and the CLI can assume such a role with an MFA code; it needs a new role and a changed workflow, so it is more overhead than GetSessionToken plus an aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition. E fails because MFA Delete applies to versioned buckets and permanent version deletes, and only the root user can enable it.

case.label: C
case.text: Writing an inline deny policy keyed on the token issue time has the same effect as revoking active sessions, so it would work; it loses because it is the manual version of the built-in revoke action and needs writing and testing. B fails because STS has no operation to revoke one session token.

case.label: B
case.text: B also uses an external ID, but one shared value given to every vendor defeats the purpose; the ID must be the unique value the vendor generated for this customer. C uses long-term credentials and D puts permissions in the wrong policy.

case.label: A
case.text: One analyzer is less work, and IAM roles are global, so a candidate could argue one Region covers the roles; but S3 buckets and KMS keys are regional and an analyzer covers only the resources in its own Region, so one analyzer misses two Regions.

case.label: A
case.text: A bucket policy for the development account would not help, because after AssumeRole the request is made by the role session in the production account, not by the development account; the role itself needs s3:GetObject. The trust policy (C) is already working since AssumeRole succeeds.
